nominative.summary: The naming form is usually the dictionary form in the singular. The plural is a separate form to learn, especially for male-person nouns.
singular: Most masculine nouns here end in a consonant (kot, dom). Many feminine nouns end in -a (książka), and many neuter nouns end in -o or -e (dziecko, miejsce). These are common shapes, not a gender test that works for every noun.
A masculine person can also have singular -a, as in kolega. Its gender still matters elsewhere in the paradigm.
plural: Non-masculine-personal plurals often use -y, -i or -e; książka → książki has -i after k. Many neuter nouns have -a (miasto → miasta).
Masculine-personal plurals use several patterns, including -i, -e and -owie, often with a changed stem: student → studenci. The exact plural should be learned with the noun.
nominative.stem: A plural may soften or reshape a stem: student → studenci. Do not make every plural by adding one ending to the dictionary form.
nominative.remember: Dziecko → dzieci is a high-frequency irregular plural. Pies → psy loses the vowel in its stem. Learn these as whole forms.

genitive.summary: Gender narrows the choice of ending, but masculine singular -a versus -u and many plural forms must be learned noun by noun.
singular: Masculine animate nouns often take -a: kot → kota. Masculine inanimate nouns may take -u (dom → domu, czas → czasu) or -a; do not infer the ending from inanimacy alone.
Many feminine -a nouns take -y (szkoła → szkoły) or -i after k/g (książka → książki). Common neuter -o nouns take -a (dziecko → dziecka).
plural: Many masculine nouns use -ów (kot → kotów), while others use -i or another form. Masculine-personal brat → braci is not made with -ów.
Many feminine and neuter nouns have no added ending, but the stem can change: książka → książek inserts e; dziecko → dzieci is irregular.
genitive.stem: The stem can change as well as the ending: pies → psa loses ie; cukier → cukru loses e. In książka → książki, k is followed by written i rather than y.
genitive.remember: Learn masculine inanimate genitives with the noun: dom → domu, czas → czasu, but chleb → chleba. This is a lexical choice, not a universal ending rule.

comparisons.note: feminine: no added ending, inserted e

dative.summary: A recipient or a dative-taking verb calls for dative; the noun's gender and stem determine its form.
singular: Masculine nouns often take -owi (przyjaciel → przyjacielowi), but a common smaller group takes -u (kot → kotu, brat → bratu).
Feminine -a nouns often take -e/-ie with a softened stem (kobieta → kobiecie); some take -y/-i. Neuter -o nouns commonly take -u (dziecko → dziecku).
plural: The broad plural ending is -om across genders: kot → kotom, książka → książkom, dziecko → dzieciom. The plural stem can still be irregular.
dative.stem: Before -e, consonants may change: kobieta → kobiecie (t → ci), książka → książce (k → c), siostra → siostrze (r → rz).
dative.remember: Pies → psu loses ie; ojciec → ojcu also changes its stem. Do not derive these by simply attaching -u.

accusative.summary: In the accusative, animacy matters in the singular and masculine-personal status matters in the plural.
singular: Masculine animate nouns normally match their genitive: kot → kota. Masculine inanimate nouns normally match nominative: dom → dom. Feminine -a nouns commonly use -ę: książka → książkę. Neuter nouns normally match nominative: dziecko → dziecko.
Masculine nouns ending in -a, such as kolega, follow a feminine-looking singular ending pattern; do not classify gender from the last letter alone.
plural: Masculine-personal nouns match genitive plural: student → studentów. Other plurals match nominative plural, including animals: kot → koty, and feminine nouns: książka → książki.
accusative.stem: When the accusative matches another case, it also shares that case's stem: pies → psa in the singular, but pies → psy in the non-masculine-personal plural.
accusative.remember: Knowing a noun's gender and whether it is animate or masculine personal is essential. A form equal to the dictionary form, such as dom or dziecko, is still a real accusative form.

instrumental.summary: Instrumental has clear common endings, with stem and spelling changes to watch for.
singular: Masculine and neuter nouns commonly take -em or -iem: kot → kotem, dziecko → dzieckiem. Feminine -a nouns commonly replace -a with -ą: książka → książką.
The written -i in dzieckiem keeps the pronunciation after k. Compare kotem without it.
plural: Most nouns use -ami: kot → kotami, książka → książkami. Some frequent nouns use -mi and a changed stem: dziecko → dziećmi.
instrumental.stem: A stem can change independently of the ending: samochód → samochodem has ó → o; pies → psem drops ie.
instrumental.remember: Learn irregular instrumental plurals as complete forms. Dziećmi is not made by adding regular -ami to dziecko.

locative.summary: Locative occurs after a preposition. Singular -e/-ie often changes the stem; -u and feminine -y/-i also occur.
singular: Many masculine and neuter nouns use -e/-ie with a softened stem: kot → kocie, miasto → mieście. Others use -u: dom → domu, dziecko → dziecku.
Many feminine -a nouns use -e/-ie with a stem change: książka → książce. Some use -y/-i instead, such as praca → pracy.
plural: -ach is a common plural ending across genders: kot → kotach, książka → książkach, dziecko → dzieciach. The stem may still change.
locative.stem: Before -e, consonants can soften: kot → kocie (t → c), książka → książce (k → c). Miasto → mieście changes more than the final vowel.
locative.remember: There is no single locative singular ending for every noun. Learn domu and dziecku as individual -u forms, alongside -e/-ie examples.

vocative.summary: Vocative addresses someone directly. Singular forms vary; plural vocative normally matches nominative plural.
singular: Masculine nouns often use -e/-ie or -u: kot → kocie, przyjaciel → przyjacielu. Feminine -a nouns often use -o: mama → mamo.
Some familiar feminine names use -u instead: Kasia → Kasiu. A person's name or title may have a form worth memorising.
plural: The plural vocative normally matches nominative plural: student → studenci, dziecko → dzieci. Masculine-personal plural forms can have their own stem changes.
vocative.stem: The ending may soften the stem: kot → kocie (t → c). Other nouns select -u without this change, such as przyjaciel → przyjacielu.
vocative.remember: Kasia → Kasiu and pan → panie are useful forms to learn whole. Neuter nouns are rarely addressed directly; their vocative generally matches nominative when used.
